methodology: METHODOLOGY · Every entry anchors to a landmark study, paper, clinical case or theoretical text. The hint explains the idea in plain language; the note names the primary publication and flags replication status, effect-size revisions and known controversies. Studies and effects carry a replicability badge — 🟢 robust · 🟡 nuanced or reduced · 🔴 failed or severely contested. Map pins mark the institution where the work was carried out.

categories.label: Theories & Models
categories.subtitle: The frameworks that organise probability, statistics, optimisation and decision-making

entries.label: Kolmogorov's Axiomatization of Probability
entries.hint: Before 1933, probability theory was a loose collection of calculating techniques with no agreed logical foundation — mathematicians even disagreed about what a 'probability' actually was. Andrey Kolmogorov showed the entire subject could be built from just three simple axioms borrowed from measure theory, instantly making probability a fully rigorous branch of mathematics rather than a set of intuitive rules of thumb.
entries.note: Kolmogorov, A.N. (1933). Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung. Berlin: Julius Springer, written while Kolmogorov was at Moscow State University. Built directly on Henri Lebesgue's measure theory, developed three decades earlier for a completely different purpose; the axiomatization is now so completely taken for granted that most working statisticians never encounter the foundational debates it resolved.

entries.label: Central Limit Theorem
entries.hint: Add together enough independent random quantities — almost regardless of their individual distributions — and the sum's distribution converges toward the familiar bell-shaped normal curve. The theorem explains why so many unrelated real-world measurements, from human heights to measurement errors, cluster into approximately the same bell shape: each is itself the sum of many small, roughly independent contributing factors.
entries.note: Laplace, P.S. (1810). 'Mémoire sur les approximations des formules qui sont fonctions de très grands nombres.' Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences de Paris. Abraham de Moivre had proved a narrower special case for coin-flip outcomes in 1733; Laplace generalised it substantially, and the fully general modern version, covering arbitrary distributions with finite variance, was not proved until Lyapunov's 1901 work using characteristic functions.

entries.label: Law of Large Numbers
entries.hint: Repeat a random experiment often enough — flip a coin, roll a die — and the average of the outcomes converges toward the theoretical expected value, with the chance of a large deviation shrinking as the number of repetitions grows. Jacob Bernoulli called this his 'golden theorem' and spent over twenty years proving it rigorously, aware it was the first result to put mathematical teeth into the everyday intuition that more data means more certainty.
entries.note: Bernoulli, J. Ars Conjectandi (1713), Basel — published eight years after Bernoulli's death by his nephew Nicolaus Bernoulli. The result proved is what's now called the 'weak' law of large numbers; the stronger 'strong' law, guaranteeing convergence with probability 1 rather than merely high probability, was not proved until Émile Borel's 1909 work and later refined by Kolmogorov.

entries.label: Bayes' Theorem
entries.hint: A formula for updating a belief's probability in light of new evidence — starting from a prior probability, then revising it using how likely the observed evidence would be under each competing hypothesis. It reframes probability as a measure of rational belief that can be systematically corrected, not only a property of physical randomness like dice or coins.
entries.note: Bayes, T. (1763). 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 53, 370–418 — published posthumously by his friend Richard Price, who found the manuscript among Bayes's papers. Pierre-Simon Laplace independently rediscovered and substantially generalised the same result a decade later, unaware of Bayes's earlier essay; the proper interpretation and use of Bayesian reasoning remains actively disputed within statistics to this day.

entries.label: Neyman–Pearson Hypothesis Testing Framework
entries.hint: Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson formalised statistical hypothesis testing as a decision procedure with two clearly named failure modes — wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type I error) and wrongly failing to reject a false one (Type II error) — and showed how to design a test minimising one error rate for any fixed tolerance of the other. This decision-theoretic framing became the version taught in most introductory statistics courses.
entries.note: Neyman, J. & Pearson, E.S. (1933). 'On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 231, 289–337, at University College London. Neyman and Pearson's decision-theoretic framework and Fisher's earlier significance-testing approach are subtly incompatible in their interpretation of what a p-value means; most textbooks today teach a hybrid of the two that neither man fully endorsed.

entries.label: Linear Programming Duality
entries.hint: Every linear optimisation problem — maximise this quantity subject to these constraints — has a paired 'dual' problem whose optimal solution gives the exact same value, viewed from the opposite direction. The duality theorem gives a practical way to certify that a proposed solution is truly optimal, without having to search the entire space of alternatives.
entries.note: Gale, D., Kuhn, H.W. & Tucker, A.W. (1951). 'Linear Programming and the Theory of Games,' in Activity Analysis of Production and Allocation, T.C. Koopmans (Ed.), Cowles Commission Monograph 13, RAND Corporation, Santa Monica. John von Neumann had communicated the core duality idea to George Dantzig in an informal 1947 conversation, connecting it directly to his own earlier minimax theorem for games, but never published it himself.

entries.label: The Minimax Theorem
entries.hint: In a two-player zero-sum game, where one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, John von Neumann proved a stable optimal strategy always exists for both sides — a way to play that minimises your maximum possible loss, which exactly matches the opponent's own optimal strategy from their side. It was the founding result that turned game theory from an informal way of talking about games into a genuine mathematical discipline.
entries.note: von Neumann, J. (1928). 'Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele.' Mathematische Annalen, 100, 295–320, written during von Neumann's time as Privatdozent at the University of Berlin. Von Neumann reportedly considered this paper, rather than any of his far more famous later work in computing, one of his personal favourites; his separate stored-program computer architecture work is covered as a figure in the computer-science folio.

entries.label: Nash Equilibrium
entries.hint: John Nash extended von Neumann's minimax result far beyond two-player zero-sum games, proving that any game with any finite number of players has at least one stable outcome where no single player can improve their own result by unilaterally changing strategy, given everyone else's choices stay fixed. This far more general equilibrium concept became the central organising idea of modern game theory.
entries.note: Nash, J. (1950). 'Equilibrium Points in n-Person Games.' Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 36(1), 48–49, based on Nash's Princeton doctoral dissertation the same year. The proof uses Kakutani's fixed-point theorem, a generalisation of Brouwer's fixed-point theorem covered in the pure-mathematics folio; Nash's later life with schizophrenia and 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize were the subject of the book and film A Beautiful Mind.

entries.label: Queueing Theory
entries.hint: Agner Krarup Erlang modelled the seemingly chaotic problem of how many telephone lines a switchboard needs to keep customers from being blocked, treating call arrivals and durations as random processes with well-defined statistical properties. His formulas let phone companies calculate, in advance, exactly how much capacity to install for any target level of service — founding an entire discipline for managing waiting lines, from call centres to hospital emergency rooms.
entries.note: Erlang, A.K. (1909). 'The Theory of Probabilities and Telephone Conversations.' Nyt Tidsskrift for Matematik B, 20, 33–39, developed while working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company. Erlang's loss formula (1917) for calculating call-blocking probability is still standard in telecommunications capacity planning over a century later, essentially unchanged.

entries.label: Modern Portfolio Theory
entries.hint: Harry Markowitz showed that an investor shouldn't judge an individual asset's risk in isolation, but should instead consider how it moves relative to everything else already in the portfolio — a volatile asset can actually reduce a portfolio's overall risk if its price swings tend to offset the others'. This reframed investing as a mathematical optimisation problem, trading expected return against portfolio-wide variance, rather than a matter of picking good individual stocks.
entries.note: Markowitz, H. (1952). 'Portfolio Selection.' The Journal of Finance, 7(1), 77–91, written at the University of Chicago. Markowitz shared the 1990 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this work; the theory assumes investors can accurately estimate future returns, variances and correlations in advance, an assumption real markets frequently violate, which later motivated the Efficient Market Hypothesis debate.

entries.label: Black–Scholes Option Pricing Theory
entries.hint: Fischer Black and Myron Scholes derived a formula for the fair price of a financial option — the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price later — based only on the current asset price, its volatility, and a few other observable quantities, with no need to predict whether the price will go up or down. The formula's core insight, dynamic hedging, remains the conceptual basis of modern derivatives pricing.
entries.note: Black, F. & Scholes, M. (1973). 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities.' Journal of Political Economy, 81(3), 637–654, developed while Black was at the University of Chicago and Scholes at MIT; Robert Merton's companion paper the same year extended the mathematics further. Scholes and Merton received the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize (Black had died in 1995 and was ineligible); the formula's constant-volatility assumption was directly implicated in the flawed risk models behind Long-Term Capital Management's 1998 collapse.

categories.label: Landmark Studies
categories.subtitle: The defining experiments — and exactly what they found

entries.label: Fisher's Statistical Methods for Research Workers
entries.hint: Ronald Fisher, working as the sole statistician at an agricultural research station, developed randomisation, blocking, and analysis of variance (ANOVA) as a unified toolkit for designing experiments that could isolate a genuine causal effect from background noise using the fewest possible test plots. The techniques he built to compare fertiliser treatments on wheat became, with only minor adaptation, the statistical backbone of clinical trials, psychology experiments, and manufacturing quality control decades later.
entries.note: Fisher, R.A. (1925). Statistical Methods for Research Workers. Edinburgh: Oliver & Boyd, and (1935) The Design of Experiments, same publisher — both written during Fisher's tenure at Rothamsted Experimental Station, Harpenden. Fisher's popularisation of the 0.05 significance threshold in these books, offered originally as a rough convention rather than a firm rule, became the rigid pass/fail line much of the discipline still argues about.

entries.label: Dantzig's Simplex Method
entries.hint: George Dantzig invented an algorithm that solves linear programming problems — optimise a linear objective subject to linear constraints — by systematically moving from one corner of the feasible region to an adjacent, better corner, until no further improvement is possible. Despite having no proven worst-case efficiency guarantee, it performs so reliably well in practice that it remained the dominant optimisation algorithm in industry for decades.
entries.note: Dantzig, G.B. (1947, first published account 1951). 'Maximization of a Linear Function of Variables Subject to Linear Inequalities,' in Activity Analysis of Production and Allocation, Cowles Commission Monograph 13. Developed while Dantzig worked as a mathematical advisor for the US Air Force in Washington, D.C. A well-known story holds that Dantzig, arriving late to a graduate class years earlier, mistook two unsolved statistics problems on the blackboard for homework and solved them both — a separate, often-conflated anecdote from well before the simplex method itself.

entries.label: von Neumann & Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
entries.hint: John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern's book extended game theory from von Neumann's earlier two-player results into a general mathematical framework for economic decision-making, and along the way rigorously derived expected utility theory — a formal justification for why rational decision-makers under uncertainty should act as if maximising an expected value at all. It is generally credited with founding game theory as a systematic field rather than a scattered set of individual results.
entries.note: von Neumann, J. & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Princeton: Princeton University Press, written at Princeton University. The 641-page book was considered forbiddingly technical on release and sold modestly at first, but its influence over subsequent decades — in economics, evolutionary biology, and political science alike — is now considered one of the most consequential works of twentieth-century applied mathematics.

entries.label: Flood and Dresher's Prisoner's Dilemma Experiment
entries.hint: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher ran an experiment at RAND in which two players repeatedly chose to 'cooperate' or 'defect' for real money, discovering that participants often cooperated far more than the theoretically dominant strategy (always defect) would predict — an early, uncomfortable hint that real human behaviour and game-theoretic rational-actor predictions could diverge sharply. Albert Tucker later formalised and named the underlying game structure the 'Prisoner's Dilemma' while giving an informal talk to a psychology audience.
entries.note: Flood, M. & Dresher, M. (1950). Unpublished RAND Corporation working paper, Santa Monica, California; Tucker's naming and prisoner-framing followed shortly after in an informal 1950 seminar, first appearing in print via later expositions. The gap between the experiment's cooperative results and the theory's predicted defection became a founding case study for behavioural game theory.

entries.label: Kelly's Criterion
entries.hint: John Kelly, a physicist at Bell Labs working on noisy communication channels, derived a formula for the optimal fraction of a bankroll to wager on a favourable bet, showing it maximises the long-run exponential growth rate of wealth rather than merely the expected value of any single bet — betting too much, even on a genuinely good bet, provably destroys wealth over repeated plays through the mathematics of compounding losses. The result, originally framed around information theory, was later adopted directly by professional gamblers and some hedge funds.
entries.note: Kelly, J.L. (1956). 'A New Interpretation of Information Rate.' Bell System Technical Journal, 35(4), 917–926, at Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey. Kelly built directly on Claude Shannon's information theory, developed at the same institution less than a decade earlier; economist Paul Samuelson published pointed objections to using the criterion for real investment decisions in the 1970s, arguing it ignores an investor's actual utility for risk, a dispute that persists in quantitative finance today.

entries.label: The Metropolis Monte Carlo Paper
entries.hint: Nicholas Metropolis and collaborators at Los Alamos devised a way to estimate the properties of a complicated probability distribution — one too difficult to compute directly — by generating a long random walk of sample points that visits each region in proportion to its actual probability, then simply averaging over the samples collected. The technique, developed originally for nuclear weapons physics calculations, became one of the most widely used computational tools across all of applied statistics and physics.
entries.note: Metropolis, N., Rosenbluth, A.W., Rosenbluth, M.N., Teller, A.H. & Teller, E. (1953). 'Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines.' Journal of Chemical Physics, 21(6), 1087–1092, run on the MANIAC computer at Los Alamos National Laboratory. W.K. Hastings generalised the algorithm in 1970, giving the now-standard 'Metropolis–Hastings' name; the method underlies Markov Chain Monte Carlo, Bayesian computation, and simulated annealing optimisation.

entries.label: Ioannidis's "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False"
entries.hint: John Ioannidis argued, using a mathematical model of how studies get run and published rather than any single new experiment, that in fields with small effect sizes, many tested hypotheses, flexible study designs, and strong pressure to publish positive results, a majority of published 'statistically significant' findings will actually turn out to be false positives. The paper became one of the most-cited and most-discussed methodology papers of the following two decades, directly fuelling the broader replication crisis debate.
entries.note: Ioannidis, J.P.A. (2005). 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False.' PLOS Medicine, 2(8), e124, written while at the University of Ioannina School of Medicine, Greece. The paper is a theoretical/probabilistic argument, not an empirical survey of actual replication rates; large-scale empirical replication projects in psychology (2015) and elsewhere subsequently found failure rates broadly consistent with Ioannidis's warning, though the exact numbers remain debated by field.

entries.label: Blackett's Circus: Operational Research in the Battle of the Atlantic
entries.hint: Physicist Patrick Blackett assembled a mixed team of scientists — nicknamed 'Blackett's Circus' — to apply statistical analysis directly to live military decisions, discovering through data alone, not intuition or tradition, that larger merchant-ship convoys suffered proportionally fewer losses than smaller ones, and that patrol aircraft painted white rather than black were spotted later by U-boats and sank more of them. It was one of the first times mathematics was used this directly to make operational, not just engineering, decisions in real time.
entries.note: Blackett, P.M.S. Coastal Command and Anti-U-Boat Warfare Operational Research Section reports, 1941–42, London, later summarised in Blackett, P.M.S. (1962). Studies of War. New York: Hill & Wang. The convoy-size finding directly overturned British Admiralty intuition that smaller convoys were safer because they were less likely to be spotted; the group's methods, once validated by outcomes, were rapidly adopted across British and then American military planning, founding operational research as an organised discipline.

entries.label: The Pascal–Fermat Correspondence
entries.hint: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged a series of letters solving the 'problem of points' — how to fairly divide the stakes of an interrupted gambling game between two players, based on each player's chances of winning had play continued — by systematically enumerating and weighing future possible outcomes rather than relying on custom or guesswork. Their correspondence is conventionally treated as the founding moment of mathematical probability theory.
entries.note: Pascal, B. & Fermat, P. de. Correspondence, July–October 1654, Paris. Girolamo Cardano had worked on related gambling probability questions roughly a century earlier in an unpublished manuscript (Liber de ludo aleae, published only in 1663), but the Pascal–Fermat exchange is what actually circulated and directly shaped the field's subsequent development, via Christiaan Huygens's 1657 treatise summarising their results for a wider audience.

entries.label: Courant's Variational Origins of the Finite Element Method
entries.hint: Richard Courant showed that certain physical equilibrium and vibration problems, normally solved with exact but intractable differential equations, could instead be approximated by breaking the problem's domain into a mesh of small simple pieces and solving a much easier variational, energy-minimisation problem over that mesh — the mathematical seed of what became the finite element method. The technique sat as a curiosity for over a decade before digital computers made mesh-based approximation genuinely practical.
entries.note: Courant, R. (1943). 'Variational Methods for the Solution of Problems of Equilibrium and Vibrations.' Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 49(1), 1–23, written at New York University. Engineers M.J. Turner, R.W. Clough, H.C. Martin and L.J. Topp independently rediscovered and named the practical 'finite element method' in 1956 for aircraft structural analysis at Boeing, unaware of Courant's earlier mathematical treatment; the two lines of work were only recognised as equivalent afterward.

entries.label: Halley's Life Table
entries.hint: Edmond Halley — better known for the comet — analysed detailed birth and death records from the city of Breslau to construct the first rigorous mortality table, calculating the probability that a person of any given age would survive to any later age. The table let, for the first time, insurance premiums and life annuities be priced according to an actual, data-derived risk rather than rough guesswork or flat, age-blind rates, founding actuarial science as a quantitative discipline.
entries.note: Halley, E. (1693). 'An Estimate of the Degrees of the Mortality of Mankind.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 17, 596–610, based on records compiled by Caspar Neumann in Breslau (now Wrocław, Poland) and analysed by Halley in London. Earlier mortality work by John Graunt (1662) had estimated London death patterns from parish records, but without Halley's rigorous age-structured survival calculations; Halley's table remained the standard reference for annuity pricing in England for over a century.

categories.label: Effects & Phenomena
categories.subtitle: Named, replicable patterns in probabilistic and statistical reasoning

entries.label: Simpson's Paradox
entries.hint: A trend that appears clearly in several separate groups of data can completely reverse direction when those groups are combined into one — a treatment can look worse than a placebo in every individual hospital, yet look better than the placebo once all the hospitals' data are pooled together. The reversal isn't a calculation error; it happens whenever a hidden third variable (like disease severity) is unevenly distributed across the groups being compared.
entries.note: Simpson, E.H. (1951). 'The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables.' Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 13(2), 238–241. The underlying arithmetic pattern had been noted earlier by Karl Pearson (1899) and George Udny Yule (1903); Simpson's name attached to it after Colin Blyth's 1972 paper popularised the term 'Simpson's Paradox.' Correcting for it requires deliberately choosing the right level of aggregation, which is not always obvious in advance — a live methodological problem, not just a historical curiosity.

entries.label: The Birthday Paradox
entries.hint: In a room of just 23 randomly chosen people, there is better than a 50% chance that two of them share a birthday — a result most people badly underestimate, since they intuitively (and wrongly) compare each person only to themselves rather than accounting for every possible pair among the group. With 70 people, the probability of a shared birthday exceeds 99.9%.
entries.note: von Mises, R. (1939). 'Über Aufteilungs- und Besetzungswahrscheinlichkeiten.' Revue de la Faculté des Sciences de l'Université d'Istanbul, 4, 145–163, written while von Mises was in exile from Nazi Germany, teaching at Istanbul University. The result is not a 'paradox' in the logical sense — nothing is actually contradictory — but a demonstration of how badly untrained intuition estimates combinatorial probabilities involving pairs rather than individuals.

entries.label: The St. Petersburg Paradox
entries.hint: A coin-flipping game keeps doubling its payout for every consecutive heads before the first tails appears, giving the game an infinite mathematical expected value — yet almost nobody would pay more than a modest, finite entry fee to play it. The mismatch between infinite expected value and obviously finite real-world willingness to pay exposed a fundamental flaw in judging decisions by expected monetary value alone.
entries.note: Bernoulli, D. (1738). 'Specimen theoriae novae de mensura sortis.' Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae, 5, 175–192, resolving a problem posed twenty-five years earlier by his cousin Nicolas Bernoulli. Daniel Bernoulli's resolution — that people maximise expected *utility*, not expected monetary value, and that utility grows more slowly than money (diminishing marginal utility) — is the direct ancestor of the expected utility theory formalised two centuries later by von Neumann and Morgenstern.

entries.label: Regression Toward the Mean
entries.hint: Extreme measurements — unusually tall parents, an athlete's career-best season, a factory's worst-ever defect rate — tend to be followed by less extreme ones, purely as a statistical consequence of measurement variability, without any underlying causal correction happening at all. Francis Galton discovered this studying inherited height: tall parents' children were, on average, shorter than their parents, and short parents' children taller — 'regressing' toward the population mean.
entries.note: Galton, F. (1886). 'Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature.' Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, 15, 246–263. Widely and easily misread as implying an active causal force pulling outcomes back toward average, rather than a purely statistical artifact of imperfect correlation between two measurements — a confusion still common in sports commentary ('the sophomore slump') and business forecasting today.

entries.label: Benford's Law
entries.hint: In an enormous range of real-world numerical datasets — river lengths, stock prices, physical constants, census figures — the leading digit is 1 roughly 30% of the time and 9 less than 5% of the time, rather than each digit appearing equally often as naive intuition would suggest. The pattern holds specifically for data spanning several orders of magnitude, and its violation is now used as one screening tool for detecting fabricated financial and election data.
entries.note: Benford, F. (1938). 'The Law of Anomalous Numbers.' Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 78(4), 551–572, based on an analysis of over 20,000 numbers from 20 different datasets, written while Benford worked as a physicist at General Electric, Schenectady. Simon Newcomb had noted the same pattern informally in 1881, observing that logarithm tables were more worn at the front (digit 1) than the back; a full mathematical explanation of exactly why the law holds was not given until Theodore Hill's 1995 proof.

entries.label: The Monty Hall Problem
entries.hint: In a game show puzzle where a contestant picks one of three doors, one hiding a prize, and the host then opens a different, empty door before offering a chance to switch — switching doubles the contestant's odds of winning, from 1/3 to 2/3, a result so counterintuitive that even many professional mathematicians initially rejected it as wrong. The trick is that the host's choice of which empty door to reveal is not random; it carries information.
entries.note: Selvin, S. (1975). 'A Problem in Probability.' The American Statistician, 29(1), 67, at the University of California, Berkeley. The problem became a national controversy in 1990 after Marilyn vos Savant answered a reader's version of it correctly in her Parade magazine column and received thousands of letters, many from PhD mathematicians, incorrectly insisting she was wrong; simulations and formal proofs subsequently vindicated her answer beyond dispute.

entries.label: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
entries.hint: A statistical model that is too simple systematically misses real patterns in the data (high bias); a model that is too flexible instead starts fitting the random noise specific to its training data, and performs poorly on new data it hasn't seen (high variance). The two error sources trade off against each other as model complexity increases, meaning the best-performing model on new data is rarely the one that fits the training data most closely.
entries.note: Geman, S., Bienenstock, E. & Doursat, R. (1992). 'Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma.' Neural Computation, 4(1), 1–58, at Brown University. The underlying decomposition of prediction error into bias and variance terms is older statistical folklore, but this paper gave it its now-standard name and rigorous treatment in the context of learning machines; the tradeoff underlies the practice of cross-validation and regularisation across all of modern statistical machine learning.

entries.label: p-Hacking
entries.hint: Given enough flexibility in how a dataset is analysed — which variables to include, when to stop collecting data, which outliers to exclude — a researcher can push almost any dataset past the conventional p<0.05 significance threshold purely by chance, without any real effect existing at all or any conscious intent to cheat. A landmark demonstration showed this could make listening to a song about ageing appear to make people literally younger, statistically speaking.
entries.note: Simmons, J.P., Nelson, L.D. & Simonsohn, U. (2011). 'False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant.' Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359–1366, at the University of Pennsylvania. The paper's own demonstration deliberately p-hacked a genuinely null result into apparent significance to make the point vividly; it became one of the direct catalysts for the pre-registration movement, requiring researchers to specify their analysis plan before seeing the data.

entries.label: The Braess Paradox
entries.hint: Adding a new road to a congested traffic network can, counterintuitively, make the average travel time for every driver worse rather than better, because individually rational route choices don't automatically add up to a collectively optimal outcome. The same underlying mathematics — that unconstrained individual optimisation can produce a worse group result than some constrained alternative — appears in electrical networks and internet routing, not just road traffic.
entries.note: Braess, D. (1968). 'Über ein Paradoxon aus der Verkehrsplanung.' Unternehmensforschung, 12(1), 258–268, at the University of Münster. Several cities have observed the effect in reverse in practice — Seoul's 2005 removal of the Cheonggyecheon elevated highway and New York's 1990 closure of 42nd Street both saw traffic conditions improve rather than worsen; the paradox is a special case of the more general gap between a Nash equilibrium and a socially optimal outcome.

categories.label: Key Concepts
categories.subtitle: The building blocks and vocabulary every student must command

entries.label: Expected Value
entries.hint: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the probability-weighted average of all its possible outcomes — not necessarily a value the quantity could ever actually take (the expected value of a die roll is 3.5), but the long-run average if the same random process were repeated indefinitely. Christiaan Huygens gave the concept its first systematic mathematical treatment, directly building on Pascal and Fermat's earlier correspondence.
entries.note: Huygens, C. (1657). De ratiociniis in ludo aleae ['On Reasoning in Games of Chance']. Leiden: Elzevir, written while Huygens was working in The Hague — the first published textbook on probability, expanding on the unpublished Pascal–Fermat correspondence he had learned of during a visit to Paris.

entries.label: Variance & Standard Deviation
entries.hint: Variance measures how spread out a dataset is around its mean, calculated as the average of each value's squared distance from that mean; the standard deviation, its square root, brings the measure back into the data's original units, making it directly interpretable. Karl Pearson coined the term 'standard deviation' and standardised the now-universal notation (σ) for it.
entries.note: Pearson, K. (1893). 'Contributions to the Mathematical Theory of Evolution.' Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 54, 329–333, at University College London. Pearson built on Gauss and Laplace's earlier, less standardised measures of dispersion; his broader statistical toolkit, including the correlation coefficient and chi-squared test, made UCL's Biometric Laboratory the era's leading centre for quantitative statistics.

entries.label: Correlation vs. Causation
entries.hint: Two variables can move together in a precise, measurable, statistically robust way without either one causing the other — both might be driven by a shared third factor, or the relationship might simply be coincidental given enough comparisons. Francis Galton gave correlation its first rigorous mathematical treatment, but the field spent the following century repeatedly relearning that a strong correlation coefficient, on its own, never distinguishes between these possibilities.
entries.note: Galton, F. (1888). 'Co-relations and their Measurement, Chiefly from Anthropometric Data.' Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 45, 135–145. Karl Pearson formalised Galton's idea into the modern correlation coefficient (the 'Pearson r') in 1896; distinguishing genuine causal relationships from mere correlation generally requires either a randomised controlled experiment or careful causal-inference methods well beyond the correlation coefficient itself.

entries.label: Statistical Significance & the p-value
entries.hint: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was actually measured, if the null hypothesis (typically, 'there is no real effect') were in fact true — it is not, despite near-universal misinterpretation, the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true. Karl Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit test was among the first tools to systematically generate such probabilities for real data.
entries.note: Pearson, K. (1900). 'On the Criterion that a Given System of Deviations from the Probable in the Case of a Correlated System of Variables is Such that It Can be Reasonably Supposed to Have Arisen from Random Sampling.' Philosophical Magazine, Series 5, 50(302), 157–175, at University College London. Ronald Fisher later popularised the p-value as a general-purpose significance measure across all of experimental statistics (see st1); the widespread conflation of 'statistically significant' with 'true, important, or large' remains one of the most persistent misunderstandings in applied statistics.

entries.label: Utility Function
entries.hint: A utility function converts outcomes — money, goods, risk, time — into a single numerical scale representing how much a decision-maker actually values them, allowing decisions under uncertainty to be modelled as maximising the expected value of utility rather than of the raw outcome itself. The idea traces to Daniel Bernoulli's resolution of the St. Petersburg Paradox, but was not placed on fully rigorous axiomatic footing until two centuries later.
entries.note: von Neumann, J. & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, Appendix, Princeton University Press — the first derivation of a utility function from a small set of explicit rationality axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, and independence), rather than simply assumed to exist. Behavioural economists, notably Kahneman and Tversky's Prospect Theory (1979), later documented systematic ways real human choices violate these axioms.

entries.label: Convexity
entries.hint: A set is convex if the straight line between any two of its points stays entirely inside it, and a function is convex if the region above its graph has this same property — a deceptively simple geometric condition that, when it holds, guarantees any locally optimal solution to an optimisation problem is automatically the globally optimal one too. This single property is what separates optimisation problems that are reliably solvable from those that are, in the worst case, computationally intractable.
entries.note: Fenchel, W. (1953). Convex Cones, Sets, and Functions. Lecture notes, Princeton University — the first systematic treatment of convex analysis as a unified subject. Convexity underlies why linear programming (see th6) is always efficiently solvable, while general non-convex optimisation, including training most large neural networks, offers no comparable global-optimum guarantee at all.

entries.label: Chebyshev's Inequality
entries.hint: For any probability distribution with a finite variance, no matter its shape, Chebyshev's inequality guarantees that the probability of a random outcome falling far from its mean is bounded — at most 1/k² of outcomes can lie more than k standard deviations away, regardless of whether the distribution is bell-shaped, skewed, or something stranger entirely. It is one of the few genuinely distribution-free tools in all of probability theory.
entries.note: Chebyshev, P.L. (1867). 'Des valeurs moyennes.' Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées, 2nd series, 12, 177–184, written at St. Petersburg University. A weaker special case had been proved by Bienaymé in 1853; the inequality's bound is loose for well-behaved distributions like the normal curve (where deviations beyond a few standard deviations are actually far rarer than the bound suggests) but remains the only guarantee available when nothing at all is known about a distribution's shape.

entries.label: Markov Property
entries.hint: A random process has the Markov property if its future depends only on its present state, not on the specific sequence of events that led there — a chess position, not the game's move history, is all that matters for predicting what happens next. Andrei Markov proved the first results about such 'memoryless' chains specifically to demonstrate that the law of large numbers doesn't require full statistical independence, only this much weaker condition.
entries.note: Markov, A.A. (1906). 'Extension of the Law of Large Numbers to Dependent Events' (Russian), Bulletin of the Physico-Mathematical Society of Kazan University, 15, 135–156, written at St. Petersburg University. Markov reportedly developed the theory partly to win an argument with fellow mathematician Pavel Nekrasov, who had claimed independence was necessary for the law of large numbers to hold; Markov chains underpin the Metropolis Monte Carlo method (see st6) and Google's PageRank algorithm.

entries.label: The Traveling Salesman Problem
entries.hint: Given a list of cities and the distances between them, find the shortest possible route that visits every city exactly once and returns to the start — a problem simple enough to state to a child, yet whose difficulty explodes so fast with the number of cities that no known algorithm can solve large instances by checking every possible route. It became one of the canonical examples used to define an entire class of computationally hard combinatorial optimisation problems.
entries.note: Menger, K. (1930). Presented as 'Das Botenproblem' ['The Messenger Problem'] at his Vienna mathematical colloquium, published in Ergebnisse eines Mathematischen Kolloquiums (1932). Hassler Whitney independently popularised the problem under its now-standard name at Princeton in the 1930s; the problem's formal classification as NP-hard — among the hardest problems in its computational complexity class — is covered in the computer-science folio.

categories.label: Methods & Approaches
categories.subtitle: The tools and paradigms that generate the field's evidence

entries.label: The Finite Element Method
entries.hint: A practical computational technique for approximating the solution to physical equilibrium and stress problems too complex to solve exactly, by breaking a structure into thousands of small, simply-shaped elements and solving a large but manageable system of equations linking them together. It turned Richard Courant's earlier abstract variational insight into an engineering workhorse, once digital computers made the underlying arithmetic feasible.
entries.note: Turner, M.J., Clough, R.W., Martin, H.C. & Topp, L.J. (1956). 'Stiffness and Deflection Analysis of Complex Structures.' Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences, 23(9), 805–823, developed at Boeing for aircraft structural analysis, independently of Courant's earlier mathematical treatment (see st10). The method is now standard across mechanical, civil, and aerospace engineering for stress analysis, heat transfer, and fluid dynamics simulation alike.

entries.label: Gradient Descent
entries.hint: To find a function's minimum, repeatedly step in the direction that decreases its value fastest at the current point — the negative of the gradient — adjusting the step size to balance speed against the risk of overshooting. Simple enough to predate computers by over a century, it remains, in more sophisticated modern forms, the core algorithm training essentially every large-scale machine learning model today.
entries.note: Cauchy, A.L. (1847). 'Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées.' Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 25, 536–538, Paris. Cauchy proposed it for solving astronomical calculation systems, with no notion of the technique's eventual role in computing; plain gradient descent converges slowly on many real problems, motivating later refinements like momentum and adaptive step sizes (stochastic gradient descent, Adam) covered in the computer-science folio's machine learning content.

entries.label: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
entries.hint: Given some observed data and a family of candidate probability models, maximum likelihood estimation picks whichever specific model within that family would have made the actually-observed data most probable. It gave statisticians a single, general-purpose principle for fitting almost any parametric model to data, replacing a previous grab-bag of ad hoc, problem-specific estimation techniques.
entries.note: Fisher, R.A. (1922). 'On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics.' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 222, 309–368. Fisher had introduced an earlier, less polished version of the idea in a 1912 undergraduate-era paper; the method's estimates are provably efficient (achieving the lowest possible variance among unbiased estimators) under fairly general conditions, a result formalised later via the Cramér–Rao bound.

entries.label: The Randomized Controlled Trial in Medicine
entries.hint: Patients were assigned to receive the antibiotic streptomycin or standard care using a randomisation method concealed even from the treating doctors — sealed, numbered envelopes — specifically to prevent unconscious bias in who received the promising new drug. It was the first modern clinical trial to combine randomisation with this kind of allocation concealment, adapting Fisher's agricultural experimental-design principles to human medicine for the first time.
entries.note: Medical Research Council (1948). 'Streptomycin Treatment of Pulmonary Tuberculosis.' British Medical Journal, 2(4582), 769–782, led by Austin Bradford Hill. Earlier trials had used alternation or haphazard assignment, which treating physicians could often predict and subtly manipulate; Bradford Hill's concealed randomisation became the methodological gold standard that essentially all subsequent drug-approval trials still follow.

entries.label: Dynamic Programming
entries.hint: For problems that can be broken into a sequence of overlapping smaller subproblems — the shortest route through a network, the optimal way to cut a piece of material — dynamic programming solves each distinct subproblem exactly once, stores the result, and reuses it, avoiding the exponential blowup of recomputing the same subproblem repeatedly. Richard Bellman's 'principle of optimality,' that an optimal overall solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems, underlies the whole technique.
entries.note: Bellman, R. (1957). Dynamic Programming. Princeton: Princeton University Press, developed at the RAND Corporation, Santa Monica. Bellman later said he chose the deliberately vague, unthreatening name 'dynamic programming' partly to disguise the mathematical research from a research-averse Secretary of Defense who controlled RAND's funding; the technique is now standard in operations research, control theory, and computer science algorithm design alike.

entries.label: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
entries.hint: To sample from a probability distribution too complicated to sample from directly, construct a Markov chain — a random process with no memory of its past beyond its current state — specifically engineered so that its long-run behaviour visits each region of the target distribution in exactly the right proportion. Running the chain long enough and then taking its later positions as samples turns an intractable distribution into one that can be explored computationally.
entries.note: Hastings, W.K. (1970). 'Monte Carlo Sampling Methods Using Markov Chains and Their Applications.' Biometrika, 57(1), 97–109, at the University of Toronto, generalising the narrower 1953 Metropolis algorithm (see st6) to a much broader class of target distributions. MCMC became the computational engine that made large-scale Bayesian statistics practically usable starting in the 1990s, once computing power caught up with the method's demands.

categories.label: Pioneers & Theorists
categories.subtitle: The researchers who shaped the discipline

entries.label: Blaise Pascal
entries.hint: A prodigy who had already invented a mechanical calculating machine by nineteen, Pascal's correspondence with Fermat solving the 'problem of points' effectively founded mathematical probability theory, though Pascal himself soon abandoned mathematics almost entirely for religious philosophy after a personal mystical experience in 1654. His triangle of binomial coefficients, though known earlier in China, Persia and India, still bears his name in the West.
entries.note: Pascal, B. Correspondence with Fermat (1654, see st9); Traité du triangle arithmétique (written 1654, published 1665). Pascal's later Pensées, an unfinished collection of philosophical and theological fragments including the famous 'Pascal's Wager' argument for believing in God under uncertainty, is itself an early application of expected-value reasoning to a decision problem.

entries.label: Abraham de Moivre
entries.hint: A French Huguenot refugee who fled religious persecution for London and never secured a permanent academic post, de Moivre supported himself for decades tutoring mathematics and consulting on gambling odds, while independently deriving the normal distribution as an approximation to the binomial — a special case of what became the Central Limit Theorem, eight decades before Laplace's general version.
entries.note: de Moivre, A. (1733). 'Approximatio ad Summam Terminorum Binomii (a+b)ⁿ in Seriem Expansi,' privately circulated supplement to his Doctrine of Chances (1718). De Moivre reportedly predicted the date of his own death by noticing he was sleeping fifteen minutes longer each night and extrapolating the arithmetic progression to zero — a story likely embellished but consistent with his lifelong habits of statistical reasoning.

entries.label: Thomas Bayes
entries.hint: A Presbyterian minister with no formal mathematical training beyond private study, Bayes never published the theorem now bearing his name — it was found among his papers after his death and brought to the Royal Society by his friend Richard Price, who wrote the accompanying introduction. Almost nothing else is known about how or why Bayes developed the result.
entries.note: Bayes, T. 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances' (1763, see th4). No portrait of Bayes reliably confirmed to be authentic survives, despite an image commonly circulated online and in textbooks under his name; Bayesian statistics as a broad philosophical and computational programme was not fully developed until Laplace's independent work and, much later, twentieth-century revivals by Harold Jeffreys and others.

entries.label: Pierre-Simon Laplace
entries.hint: Called the 'French Newton' by contemporaries, Laplace generalised nearly every foundational result in early probability theory — the Central Limit Theorem, Bayesian inference, and the mathematics of celestial mechanics — while also serving as a government minister under Napoleon, who reportedly dismissed him from the post for 'bringing the spirit of the infinitely small into public administration.'
entries.note: Laplace, P.S. Théorie analytique des probabilités (1812), incorporating his 1810 Central Limit Theorem proof (see th2). Laplace independently rediscovered and substantially extended Bayes's theorem, unaware of Bayes's earlier posthumous essay; famously, when Napoleon asked why his celestial mechanics work made no mention of God, Laplace reportedly replied that he 'had no need of that hypothesis.'

entries.label: Jacob Bernoulli
entries.hint: The eldest of a remarkable Swiss mathematical dynasty that produced eight notable mathematicians across three generations, Jacob Bernoulli spent the last two decades of his life obsessively working to rigorously prove what he called his 'golden theorem' — that repeated trials converge toward a true underlying probability — a result now called the Law of Large Numbers, published only after his death.
entries.note: Bernoulli, J. Ars Conjectandi (1713, see th3). Jacob's younger brother Johann Bernoulli was also a major mathematician and frequent bitter rival, publicly feuding over priority disputes; Jacob's nephew Nicolaus Bernoulli later posed the St. Petersburg Paradox that Jacob's own nephew Daniel Bernoulli resolved decades afterward (see ef3).

entries.label: Ronald Fisher
entries.hint: Working essentially alone as the statistician at an agricultural research station, Fisher single-handedly created most of the modern toolkit of experimental statistics — randomisation, analysis of variance, maximum likelihood estimation, and the popularised p-value — while also being one of the twentieth century's most influential (and most scientifically discredited) advocates of eugenics, a fact modern statistics organisations have publicly grappled with in recent years.
entries.note: Fisher, R.A. Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925, see st1); 'On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics' (1922, see me3). Fisher and Karl Pearson, and later Fisher and Jerzy Neyman, conducted some of statistics' most bitter and consequential public disputes over the correct foundations of the field, disputes whose unresolved tensions still shape how statistics is taught and used today.

entries.label: Jerzy Neyman
entries.hint: Working with Egon Pearson (son of Karl Pearson) at University College London, Neyman built a rigorous decision-theoretic alternative to Fisher's significance-testing approach, explicitly naming and formalising the two distinct ways a hypothesis test can go wrong. Neyman and Fisher's disagreement over the philosophical foundations of hypothesis testing was intense and personal, and the hybrid method most textbooks now teach was fully endorsed by neither man.
entries.note: Neyman, J. & Pearson, E.S. 'On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses' (1933, see th5). Neyman emigrated to the United States in 1938, founding an influential statistics program at the University of California, Berkeley, where he later developed confidence intervals as a companion concept to hypothesis testing.

entries.label: Andrey Kolmogorov
entries.hint: Beyond giving probability theory its modern axiomatic foundation, Kolmogorov made foundational contributions across an extraordinarily wide range of mathematics — turbulence, computational complexity, algorithmic information theory — while training a school of Soviet mathematicians at Moscow State University that dominated the field for decades under difficult political conditions.
entries.note: Kolmogorov, A.N. Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1933, see th1). Kolmogorov's later work defining the complexity of a string as the length of its shortest possible describing program — now called Kolmogorov complexity — was developed independently around the same time by Ray Solomonoff and Gregory Chaitin, and is covered in the systems-and-complexity folio.

entries.label: Agner Krarup Erlang
entries.hint: A largely self-taught mathematician working directly for the Copenhagen Telephone Company rather than any university, Erlang founded the entire field of queueing theory to solve a specific, urgent commercial problem — how many telephone circuits does a switchboard actually need — and his practical, industry-driven approach to mathematics became a model for what later grew into operational research.
entries.note: Erlang, A.K. 'The Theory of Probabilities and Telephone Conversations' (1909, see th9). The 'erlang,' a dimensionless unit measuring offered telecommunications traffic load, is named after him and remains in standard use in telecommunications engineering over a century later.

entries.label: Florence Nightingale
entries.hint: Better remembered as the founder of modern nursing, Nightingale was also a pioneering statistician who invented a striking circular chart — the 'polar area diagram,' now sometimes called a coxcomb chart — specifically to show British Parliament and army officials, who she believed wouldn't read tables, that vastly more Crimean War soldiers died from preventable disease and poor sanitation than from combat wounds.
entries.note: Nightingale, F. (1858). Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency, and Hospital Administration of the British Army. London: Harrison and Sons. Elected the first female member of the Royal Statistical Society in 1858, the same year this report appeared; her statistical advocacy directly drove major British Army sanitary reforms in the years that followed.

entries.label: George Dantzig
entries.hint: Developed the simplex algorithm while working as a mathematical advisor to the US Air Force, tasked with mechanising the planning and scheduling problems the military had previously solved by slow, informal committee deliberation. Dantzig later moved to Stanford, where he continued developing linear and large-scale optimisation for decades, and repeatedly downplayed the (partly true, partly exaggerated) legend of solving 'unsolved homework problems' as a student.
entries.note: Dantzig, G.B. 'Maximization of a Linear Function of Variables Subject to Linear Inequalities' (1947/1951, see st2). Dantzig's simplex method is regularly ranked among the most influential algorithms of the twentieth century by computing historians, given its vast use across logistics, manufacturing, airline scheduling, and finance.

entries.label: Harry Markowitz
entries.hint: A doctoral student looking for a dissertation topic, Markowitz was struck by the realisation that finance had no rigorous mathematical theory connecting an individual investment's risk to its effect on an entire portfolio's overall risk — his solution, built almost entirely from geometry and calculus rather than economics, launched quantitative finance as an academic discipline.
entries.note: Markowitz, H. 'Portfolio Selection' (1952, see th10). Markowitz has said his own committee's economics faculty initially doubted whether the dissertation, being mathematics rather than economics, should even be approved; he shared the 1990 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Merton Miller and William Sharpe.

entries.label: John Nash
entries.hint: Nash's twenty-seven-page doctoral dissertation, written at twenty-one, generalised game theory from von Neumann's narrow two-player zero-sum case to essentially any competitive situation with any number of players — then Nash spent three decades battling schizophrenia, largely absent from mathematics, before recovering enough to share the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize for the work.
entries.note: Nash, J. 'Equilibrium Points in n-Person Games' (1950, see th8). Nash's later life and illness were the subject of Sylvia Nasar's 1998 biography A Beautiful Mind and the 2001 film of the same name, both of which took significant dramatic liberties with the underlying facts of his career and personal life.

categories.label: Debates & Open Questions
categories.subtitle: Live controversies — where the field is actively contesting the evidence

entries.label: Should p<0.05 Be Abandoned?
entries.hint: The conventional 0.05 significance threshold, originally offered by Fisher as a rough convention rather than a firm rule, has become a rigid pass/fail line that critics argue encourages exactly the p-hacking and selective reporting behind the replication crisis. Proponents of keeping some fixed threshold counter that abandoning it entirely, without a workable replacement, would simply remove the one piece of friction currently discouraging researchers from reporting any result as meaningful.
entries.note: American Statistical Association (2016). 'Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values.' The American Statistician, 70(2), 129–133, Alexandria, Virginia — the ASA's first-ever formal statement on a statistical practice question. A 2019 follow-up special issue and an open letter signed by over 800 scientists went further, calling to 'retire statistical significance' altogether; no consensus alternative (confidence intervals, Bayes factors, effect-size reporting) has been adopted as a full replacement.

entries.label: Frequentist vs. Bayesian Statistics
entries.hint: Frequentist statistics defines probability as a long-run frequency across repeated trials and treats unknown parameters as fixed but unknown; Bayesian statistics treats probability as a degree of belief that can attach to a parameter itself, updated via Bayes' theorem as evidence arrives. The two schools can give different answers to the same question and, more fundamentally, disagree about what a probability statement about a hypothesis even means.
entries.note: Jeffreys, H. (1939). Theory of Probability. Oxford: Clarendon Press, written at the University of Cambridge as an explicit Bayesian countermanifesto to Fisher and Neyman–Pearson's frequentist dominance of the field. Computational advances (see me6) made full Bayesian analysis practical outside toy problems only from the 1990s onward; most modern statisticians now use both frameworks situationally rather than treating the choice as a fixed ideological commitment.

entries.label: Does Nash Equilibrium Predict Real Behavior?
entries.hint: Nash equilibrium assumes players are perfectly rational and correctly anticipate each other's strategies, but repeated laboratory experiments — starting with Flood and Dresher's own Prisoner's Dilemma study — found real human choices systematically deviating from the theory's predictions, cooperating more, and reasoning less exhaustively, than pure rational-actor models expect. Behavioural economists argue this makes classical game theory a poor predictive tool for real decisions; defenders argue it remains the right normative benchmark even when descriptively imperfect.
entries.note: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk.' Econometrica, 47(2), 263–291, written while Tversky was at Stanford University. Prospect Theory's empirically documented loss aversion and probability-weighting distortions directly contradict the expected-utility axioms underlying Nash equilibrium and von Neumann–Morgenstern rationality; Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize for this work (Tversky had died in 1996 and was ineligible).

entries.label: Is the Efficient Market Hypothesis True?
entries.hint: The Efficient Market Hypothesis claims that asset prices already fully reflect all publicly available information, meaning no investor can reliably beat the market's average return except by luck or by taking on extra risk. Behavioural finance researchers counter with well-documented, persistent pricing anomalies — momentum effects, bubbles, systematic overreaction — that a fully efficient market should not allow to survive competition from rational arbitrageurs.
entries.note: Fama, E.F. (1965). 'The Behavior of Stock-Market Prices.' Journal of Business, 38(1), 34–105, at the University of Chicago, formalised further in Fama's 1970 review paper defining the weak, semi-strong and strong forms of efficiency. Fama shared the 2013 Nobel Memorial Prize alongside Robert Shiller, a leading empirical critic of market efficiency — an unusual case of the prize being split between the architect of a theory and one of its most prominent challengers.

entries.label: Did Quantitative Risk Models Cause the 2008 Financial Crisis?
entries.hint: A statistical formula for estimating the correlated default risk of bundled mortgage securities became embedded in trillions of dollars of Wall Street risk models, based on a mathematically convenient assumption about how those risks moved together that turned out to fail catastrophically exactly when it mattered most, during the 2008 crash. Whether the failure reflects a fundamental flaw in quantitative risk modelling itself, or simply reckless misuse of a model well beyond the assumptions it was built on, remains contested among economists and mathematicians alike.
entries.note: Li, D.X. (2000). 'On Default Correlation: A Copula Function Approach.' Journal of Fixed Income, 9(4), 43–54. The formula's real-world failure was widely publicised in Salmon, F. (2009). 'Recipe for Disaster: The Formula That Killed Wall Street.' Wired, 17(3) — a title Li himself has publicly disputed as overstating a single model's role in a much broader systemic failure involving underwriting standards, leverage, and regulatory gaps.

entries.label: Ergodicity Economics: Should Expected Utility Theory Be Replaced?
entries.hint: Classical expected utility theory averages outcomes across many hypothetical parallel copies of a decision-maker (an ensemble average); Ole Peters argues the mathematically correct question for a single real person making repeated decisions over time is instead how their own wealth grows along one single time sequence (a time average) — and that for many realistic wagers, including a variant of the St. Petersburg game, the two averages give sharply different, sometimes opposite, answers about what a rational actor should do.
entries.note: Peters, O. (2011). 'Optimal Leverage from Non-Ergodicity.' Quantitative Finance, 11(11), 1593–1602, at the London Mathematical Laboratory. Peters argues the ensemble-average framework has been implicitly mistaken for the time-average one throughout economics since Daniel Bernoulli's own 1738 resolution of the St. Petersburg Paradox; mainstream economists have responded with a mix of interest and skepticism about how much of standard decision theory the reframing actually overturns in practice.

entries.label: The Replication Crisis
entries.hint: A large-scale, pre-registered effort to redo 100 published psychology experiments found that only about 36% produced a statistically significant result the second time, even using the original materials and larger sample sizes — a result that ignited a broader crisis of confidence across experimental science generally, not psychology alone. Debate continues over how much of the gap reflects genuinely false original findings versus legitimate differences in samples, settings, and unavoidable statistical noise between the original and replication studies.
entries.note: Open Science Collaboration (2015). 'Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science.' Science, 349(6251), aac4716, coordinated by the Center for Open Science, Charlottesville, Virginia. Similar large-scale replication concerns have since been documented in cancer biology, economics, and machine learning research; pre-registration, larger standard sample sizes, and open data-sharing requirements are the field's main proposed structural fixes, though adoption remains uneven across disciplines.

entries.label: Can NP-Hard Optimization Problems Be Solved Well Enough in Practice?
entries.hint: The travelling salesman problem is NP-hard, meaning no known algorithm solves every possible instance efficiently as the number of cities grows — yet sophisticated modern solvers have proven the exact optimal route for real instances with tens of thousands of cities, a scale naive worst-case theory would suggest should be hopeless. Whether this genuinely closes the gap between theoretical intractability and practical usability, or whether it merely reflects that real-world instances are unrepresentatively easy compared to adversarial worst cases, remains an open question with no settled answer.
entries.note: Applegate, D., Bixby, R., Chvátal, V. & Cook, W. (2006). Solved an 85,900-city instance to proven optimality using the Concorde TSP solver, at Georgia Institute of Technology, taking roughly 136 CPU-years of computation distributed across many processors. Concorde and similar branch-and-cut solvers combine exact optimisation with problem-specific heuristics; the underlying NP-hardness classification itself is covered in the computer-science folio's P vs NP debate.

categories.label: Applications
categories.subtitle: Where the science leaves the lab

entries.label: The Equitable Life Assurance Society
entries.hint: The Equitable Life Assurance Society was the first insurance company to set its life-insurance premiums using an actual age-based mortality table and compound interest calculations, rather than flat, age-blind rates that had previously made insurance either unprofitable for insurers or badly overpriced for younger customers. It turned Halley's and de Moivre's earlier purely mathematical mortality work into a commercially viable, mathematically sound industry for the first time.
entries.note: Founded 1762, London, with actuarial calculations by James Dodson and, after his death, William Morgan, built on the mortality-table methods of Halley (see st11) and de Moivre. The company's scientifically-priced approach proved so much more sustainable than its flat-rate competitors that it became the template the entire life insurance industry converged on over the following century.

entries.label: Wald's Aircraft Survivorship Bias Correction
entries.hint: The US military wanted to know where to add armor to bombers, based on a survey of bullet-hole locations on aircraft that had returned from missions — the obvious answer was to reinforce the areas hit most often. Abraham Wald pointed out this reasoning was backward: the planes in the survey had survived their damage, so the truly dangerous hit locations were the ones missing entirely from the data, on the planes that never made it back, and armor belonged exactly where the surviving planes showed the fewest hits.
entries.note: Wald, A. (1943). Memoranda for the Statistical Research Group, Columbia University, New York, prepared for the US Navy's Center for Naval Analyses (unpublished at the time; later collected and republished in Wald's Selected Papers, 1980). Wald's reasoning is now the canonical textbook example of survivorship bias, a systematic error from analysing only the surviving members of a population while ignoring those that were selected out.

entries.label: Epidemiological SIR Modeling
entries.hint: The SIR model divides a population into three groups — Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered — and describes how people move between them over time using a small system of differential equations, capturing the core dynamics of an epidemic (including why outbreaks eventually decline even before everyone has been infected) with remarkably few assumptions. Numerically solving these equations for different starting conditions became the basic mathematical scaffolding underneath essentially all subsequent epidemic forecasting, including during COVID-19.
entries.note: Kermack, W.O. & McKendrick, A.G. (1927). 'A Contribution to the Mathematical Theory of Epidemics.' Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115(772), 700–721, at the Royal College of Physicians Laboratory, Edinburgh. The original model's simplifying assumptions — a well-mixed, closed population with no births, deaths, or behavioural change — have been extensively relaxed in later variants (SEIR, network-based, and agent-based models) to better match real outbreak data.

entries.label: Google's PageRank Algorithm
entries.hint: PageRank ranks web pages by modelling a hypothetical user randomly clicking links forever, treating the web as a giant Markov chain, and computing each page's long-run probability of being the one that random surfer lands on at any given moment — a page linked to by many other important pages inherits importance itself, recursively. It gave Google's early search results a decisive quality advantage over competitors ranking pages mainly by simple keyword-matching frequency.
entries.note: Page, L. & Brin, S. (1998). 'The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web.' Stanford InfoLab Technical Report, Stanford University. The algorithm computes the dominant eigenvector of a matrix derived from the web's link structure, mathematically equivalent to finding a Markov chain's stationary distribution; modern search ranking has since layered hundreds of additional signals on top, but the core link-graph insight remains foundational.

entries.label: Quantitative Trading and the First Statistical Arbitrage Funds
entries.hint: Edward Thorp, having already used probability theory to beat casino blackjack, applied the same rigorous, edge-calculating mindset to financial markets, using mathematical mispricing models and the Kelly Criterion for position-sizing to run what is generally credited as the first fully quantitative hedge fund. It demonstrated that a fund could generate consistent returns from mathematical modelling of price relationships alone, without any traditional fundamental analysis of the underlying businesses.
entries.note: Thorp, E.O. & Kassouf, S.T. (1967). Beat the Market: A Scientific Stock Market System. New York: Random House, followed by the founding of Princeton-Newport Partners in 1969, Newport Beach, California. The fund reportedly achieved a roughly 15% annualised return with far lower volatility than the broader stock market over nearly two decades, directly inspiring the later, much larger wave of quantitative hedge funds including Renaissance Technologies.

entries.label: A/B Testing at Web Scale
entries.hint: Large technology companies run randomised controlled trials continuously and at massive scale on their live products — showing one version of a webpage or feature to one random slice of users and a different version to another, then measuring which version performs better on a specific metric — turning Fisher's century-old agricultural experimental design principles into millions of simultaneous, automated, real-time business experiments.
entries.note: Kohavi, R., Henne, R.M. & Sommerfield, D. (2007). 'Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers Not to the HiPPO.' Proceedings of KDD 2007, Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington. Kohavi's subsequent work publicised numerous cases of small, seemingly trivial changes producing large, statistically robust revenue effects at scale — findings that are only trustworthy given a properly randomised, adequately powered experimental design, exactly the standard Fisher and Bradford Hill established decades earlier.
